content: Women who undergo surgical treatment for epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) often experience menopausal symptoms due to the abrupt loss of ovarian function caused by surgery and chemotherapy. These symptoms can include hot flashes, sleep disturbances, difficulty concentrating, sexual dysfunction, vaginal dryness, and an increased risk of osteoporosis. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is considered the most effective treatment for alleviating these symptoms, but its safety in women with EOC has been a subject of concern. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of HRT in managing menopausal symptoms in women who have undergone surgery for EOC. To achieve this, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to June 2019. They also reviewed conference reports and trial registries, with no restrictions on language. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women of any age or menopausal status who had undergone surgery for EOC and were treated with any HRT regimen, compared to placebo or no hormone therapy. Trials comparing different HRT regimens or durations were also included. Two independent reviewers identified studies that met the inclusion criteria and extracted data using Covidence. They assessed the methodological quality of the studies and analyzed the data. Out of 2617 titles screened, only three studies, involving a total of 350 women, met the inclusion criteria. Two of these studies included both premenopausal and postmenopausal women, while the third study focused exclusively on premenopausal women. The participants ranged in age from 20 to 89.6 years, with a median follow-up period of 31.4 months to 19.1 years. The studies were conducted in Europe, South Africa, and China, and included women with various stages and histological subtypes of EOC, except for stage IV disease, which was excluded in one study. The studies employed different HRT regimens, including conjugated estrogen with or without medroxyprogesterone and with or without nylestriol, administered via oral, patch, or implant methods. Comparisons were made between women who received HRT and those who did not. The studies were found to have a low or unclear risk of selection and reporting bias but were at high risk for performance, detection, and attrition bias. The certainty of the evidence was rated as low for overall survival and progression-free survival, and very low for quality of life, breast cancer incidence, transient ischemic attack (TIA), cerebrovascular accident (CVA), and myocardial infarction (MI). A meta-analysis of the included studies suggested that HRT may improve overall survival, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 0.93; 350 participants, 3 studies; low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence for quality-of-life improvement was very uncertain, as only one study assessed this outcome using the EORTC-C30 questionnaire. The results showed a mean difference of 13.67 points higher (95% CI 9.26 to 18.08 higher; 1 study; 75 participants; very low-certainty evidence). HRT appeared to have little or no effect on progression-free survival (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.01; 275 participants, 2 studies; low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding the impact of HRT on the incidence of breast cancer, TIA, CVA, and MI was also very uncertain. For breast cancer, the risk ratio (RR) was 2.00 (95% CI 0.19 to 21.59; 225 participants, 2 studies; very low-certainty evidence). For TIA, the RR was 5.00 (95% CI 0.24 to 102.42; 150 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence). For CVA, the RR was 0.67 (95% CI 0.11 to 3.88; 150 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence). For MI, the RR was 0.20 (95% CI 0.01 to 4.10; 150 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence). None of the included studies reported on the incidence of gallstones. In conclusion, HRT may slightly improve overall survival in women who have undergone surgical treatment for EOC, but the certainty of the evidence is low. HRT may have little or no effect on quality of life, progression-free survival, or the incidence of breast cancer, TIA, CVA, and MI, but the evidence is of very low certainty. The findings of this review are limited by the imprecision and incompleteness of the reported outcomes, and the results should be interpreted with caution. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to provide more robust evidence, as this is a critical issue for women experiencing menopausal symptoms after EOC treatment. Currently, the evidence is insufficient to definitively support or refute the potential harms of HRT in this population.
